contributions.item_title_en: 6. Reform UK Debate: Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board health visitor pay dispute
contributions.text_english:
In Rhondda and Ogmore, a health visitor is often the first to notice a baby not feeding, a mother not coping, a home not safe. I accept that the board is the employer and banding must follow NHS job evaluation—the Cabinet Minister cannot sign a payslip. But this dispute has outlasted three First Ministers, and the fourth signed the demand himself—a joint open letter, on 17 April, calling for band 7. Health visitors have now publicly called on him to honour that support. Unite said the board's grading matched the roles to band 7. The board says its revaluation contains band 6. Publish the date, job descriptions, evaluation, records, scores and review rights; explain the differences. That is where a fair offer starts.

Amendment 4 replaces a call for immediate action with recognition of negotiations and the Chief Nursing Officer for Wales's review. In August, the health unions refused to take part in that job description work. Their reason: social partnership has broken down.

My freedom of information request asked whether maternity staff were deployed into health visiting between 23 February and 4 August, when Tirion's suspension was announced. The board's 8 September response did not address that question. My 9 September follow-up requested an answer by 23 September.

Cabinet Minister, on 17 June, you told this Chamber you'd expect the parties to get back around the table. Three months later, what has your personal intervention achieved? What still prevents agreement? When will that review report? And what has this Government done in four months to act on the First Minister's own signature?

I ask for three commitments. First, within 14 days, publish the banding records and a resolution timetable naming who is accountable. Secondly, publish verified monthly figures for contacts due, completed and outstanding, alongside safeguarding referrals by council area and a recovery plan prioritising children at greatest risk. Thirdly, demonstrate that cover arrangements are safe, supervised and do not weaken other services. Families need to know when help will reach them. Staff need to know when their case will be decided. This Government needs to answer both. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
contributions.text_english: I would like to declare an interest, having worked for South Wales Fire and Rescue Service for over 20 years. First Minister, I thank our firefighters, control staff and support teams. On 13 August, joint fire control handled over 1,000 calls. At one point, south Wales crews faced 14 wildfires simultaneously. Afan Ogwr Rhondda needs well-trained crews, the right equipment and reliable water supplies, even in drought. On 23 July, your Cabinet Minister announced a review of firefighting capability and costs. Will you publish a costed plan by 31 October, agreed with all three fire services, identifying what must improve, who is responsible, and what will be delivered before next spring? Your Government extended the intervention in south Wales, where commissioners set the levy paid by local councils. Will your draft budget fund those improvements so councils are not left to meet the additional costs? Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
contributions.text_english: Nobody in this Chamber disputes that preventing illness is better than treating it. But look at the evidence in my constituency. Swansea bay has been under targeted intervention for cancer since 24 January, and on the latest published figures, its bowel screening uptake is the lowest in Wales, at around 57 per cent in the most deprived communities, compared with around 72 per cent in the least deprived. Prevention is falling short precisely where it is needed most. Analysis by the future generations commissioner also found that less than 10 per cent of the previous Welsh Government's budget was directed towards evidence-based primary prevention. Warm words about prevention have never been in short supply in this Chamber; budgets and screening programmes have. So, Deputy Minister, will your Government do better? When will eligible people across Wales begin receiving invitations for the national lung cancer screening programme? And will the first budget increase the proportion spent on evidence-based primary prevention? Thank you.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
contributions.text_english: I respect the Welsh language and recognise its importance to our national heritage, but respect for the language does not remove the duty to demonstrate value for money. My constituents in Afan Ogwr Rhondda expect evidence that public spending delivers real outcomes, not simply larger budgets. Where millions of pounds are being invested in promoting the Welsh language, every pound of taxpayers' money should deliver measurable results and genuine value. Can the Cabinet Minister, therefore, explain what measurable evidence the Welsh Government has that this investment is increasing the everyday use of Welsh in communities such as Afan Ogwr Rhondda, rather than simply expanding programme strategies and administration? Will she commit to publishing, constituency by constituency, how much public money has been spent, what outcomes have been achieved and how value for money has been assessed, so that this Senedd can judge successfully on evidence, not aspiration? Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. It is with great sadness that I rise to pay tribute to Caroline Jones, a former Member of the Senedd and a woman whose courage, kindness and dedication to others left a lasting mark on Wales.

Caroline was, above all else, a public servant. Throughout her life, she devoted herself to helping others, supporting charities, veterans, homeless people, women's refuges, children's organisations, and countless community causes. She gave her time generously and worked tirelessly to improve the lives of those around her.

Her commitment to others was perhaps most evident in her support for women facing breast cancer. She faced that battle herself. Caroline became a mentor and source of hope for many women confronting the same diagnosis. She showed extraordinary courage, refusing to allow illness to define her life or limit her ambitions. Indeed, one of the most remarkable examples of her resilience was her election to this Senedd while continuing treatment for cancer. That achievement reflected not only her determination, but also her unwavering belief in public service and her desire to make a difference.

Caroline was also a proud advocate for veterans, inspired by her father's military service and strengthened by her husband's distinguished career in the armed forces. She championed those who had served our country and never missed an opportunity to support their causes.

Those who knew Caroline speak of her warmth, her generosity, her sense of humour and her ability to make people feel valued and welcome. She touched countless lives through friendship, compassion and simple acts of kindness.

Today we remember not only a former Member of this Senedd, but a remarkable woman whose legacy of courage, service and kindness will endure. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with her husband, Alun, her family, her friends and all those lives she touched. May she rest in peace.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality
contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for the question. Food poverty is a serious issue, but it cannot be an excuse to lower food standards or short-change Welsh farmers. Earlier this year, it emerged that Welsh councils were serving schoolchildren chicken imported from Thailand and China—99 nine per cent of supply in Merthyr Tydfil and 87 per cent in Caerphilly. That is difficult to justify when Welsh farmers already meet some of the highest animal welfare and food production standards in the world, yet are expected to compete on an uneven playing field. Bridgend has shown that there is no justification for this failure, sourcing 100 per cent UK chicken for its schools within the very same funding envelope and procurement framework. So, will the Cabinet Secretary accept that public money should never be used to buy food produced to standards that would not be permitted in Wales, and will the Welsh Government now reform procurement rules and require full transparency on food provenance, so parents know exactly where the food served in Welsh schools comes from? Thank you.
